questions.q: Ritu views a drop of pond water and sees one cell that swims, takes in food and divides on its own. She then views a thin slice of a rice leaf. Which statement fits what the chapter says about the two slides?
questions.a: The swimming cell does every function alone; in the leaf, groups of cells share them. An amoeba-like unicellular organism has a single cell doing all functions; the multicellular leaf has groups of cells with different functions.
o: The swimming cell does every function alone; in the leaf, groups of cells share them
Both slides show organisms in which a single cell performs all the life functions together
The swimming cell has formed tissues and divides its labour, but the leaf cells have not formed any
Both slides show tissues, because every living cell counts as a tissue by itself in the chapter

questions.q: In the human arm, the following are listed in jumbled order: biceps muscle, a single muscle cell, the muscular system of the body, a group of similar muscle cells, a whole person. Which order runs from the smallest level to the largest?
questions.a: single muscle cell, group of similar muscle cells, biceps muscle, muscular system, whole person. Cells form a tissue, tissues form an organ, organs form an organ system and organ systems form the organism.
o: single muscle cell, group of similar muscle cells, biceps muscle, muscular system, whole person
group of similar muscle cells, single muscle cell, biceps muscle, whole person, muscular system
single muscle cell, biceps muscle, group of similar muscle cells, muscular system, whole person
single muscle cell, group of similar muscle cells, muscular system, biceps muscle, whole person

questions.q: Gagan says, 'All animals can move, so animals cannot have any immobile member.' Which reply is consistent with the chapter?
questions.a: The chapter says animals move in general and names sponges as immobile ones. The statement 'animals can move' is general, and the chapter itself gives sponges as the immobile exception.
o: The chapter says animals move in general and names sponges as immobile ones
The chapter agrees, because animal cells have no rigid wall and so every animal must move
The chapter says all immobile living things are plants, so a sponge must be a plant
The chapter says sponges move only after their cells grow a rigid wall around them

questions.q: Which of the following is NOT given in the chapter as a reason why plants and animals evolved different tissues?
questions.a: Plants have no tissues for carrying food and water, but animals do.. The chapter says both plants and animals have distinct tissues for transporting food and water, so this reason is wrong; the others are the chapter's reasons.
o: Plants have no tissues for carrying food and water, but animals do.
Most plants stay fixed and need support, while most animals move about.
Plant cells have a rigid wall, while animal cells can change shape easily.
Animals digest food from outside sources, while plants use sunlight to make food.

questions.q:
Read three statements about tissues.
Statement 1: A tissue is formed when cells of several unlike types are placed together.
Statement 2: Formation of different tissues leads to division of labour, which makes the body more efficient.
Statement 3: In amoeba, one cell performs all the functions of life.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 and 3 only. A tissue is a group of similar cells doing a specific function, so statement 1 is false; statements 2 and 3 are correct.
o: 2 and 3 only
1 only
1 and 2 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Animal cells can change their shape easily.
Reason (R): Animal cells are enclosed by a rigid cell wall that lets them bend without breaking.
questions.a: A is true but R is false. A is true, but animal cells lack a rigid wall; that absence, not a wall, is what lets them change shape.
o: A is true but R is false
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match each situation (Column I) with the level of organisation it describes (Column II).
Column I: 1. A pond organism whose single cell feeds, moves and divides  2. A thousand similar cells in the stomach wall that all contract to churn food  3. The stomach, intestine and other organs that together handle food  4. The biceps, which has muscle, nerve, connective and blood tissue together
Column II: a. Organ  b. Organ system  c. Tissue  d. Unicellular organism
questions.a: 1-d, 2-c, 3-b, 4-a. One cell doing everything is a unicellular organism, similar cells doing one job form a tissue, several organs working together form an organ system, and a structure combining several tissue types is an organ.

questions.q: The biceps of the arm contains muscle tissue, nerve tissue, connective tissue and blood. Because it combines more than one type of tissue, it is called an ___.
questions.a: organ

questions.q:
A banyan tree and an amoeba are compared.
(a) Explain why the amoeba can manage without tissues.
(b) Using your answer to (a), state what the banyan gains from having different tissues.
questions.a: (a) In an amoeba a single cell performs all the functions of life, so no division of work among groups of cells is needed. (b) In the banyan different groups of cells do different jobs, so there is division of labour, which increases efficiency and lets the body carry out complex life processes.
s: (a) one cell performs all functions, so no tissues needed
(b) division of labour gives efficiency and complex life processes

questions.q:
Two cells are seen under a microscope: cell X has a rigid wall around it and cell Y has none and has changed its shape to squeeze between neighbours.
(a) Which cell is more likely from an organism fixed in one place? Give the reason from the chapter.
(b) Which organism's body is better suited to locomotion because of its cells, and why?
questions.a: (a) Cell X: most plants are fixed in one place and need support, and the rigid wall gives strength and rigidity. (b) The organism with cell Y: without a rigid wall the cells change shape easily, and this flexibility makes the body suitable for locomotion.
s: (a) cell X, fixed organisms need support from a rigid wall
(b) cell Y, shape change supports locomotion

questions.q:
Ria counts 300 cells on a slide. All are alike in structure and all store starch.
(a) Can this group be called a tissue? State the condition from the chapter that it meets.
(b) She now mixes in 300 cells of a different structure and function. Can the mixed lot of 600 cells be called a single tissue? Give the reason.
questions.a: (a) Yes, a tissue is a group of cells similar in structure that work together to perform a specific function, and these cells do. (b) No, the mixed lot has two kinds of cells with different structure and function, so it is not one group of similar cells working for a specific function.
s: (b) no: two different cell types are not one tissue

questions.q:
Rohit writes the order 'tissue, cell, organ, organism, organ system'.
(a) Correct his order from smallest to largest.
(b) Name the first level in your corrected order at which more than one type of tissue is present.
questions.a: (a) Cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism. (b) The organ, because more than one type of tissue forms an organ.
s: (a) correct sequence cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism
(b) organ has more than one tissue type

questions.q: True or False: Since one amoeba cell can do everything, a multicellular organism would be even more efficient if all its cells did all the functions of life, with no tissues. Give the reason.
questions.a: False. The chapter says different tissues lead to division of labour, which increases the efficiency of the body and lets it carry out complex life processes; cells all doing every job would lose that gain.
s: Reason: division of labour among tissues raises efficiency

questions.q: Anil says, 'In every multicellular organism each cell performs all the functions of life, just as in an amoeba.' Is he right? Explain.
questions.a: No. It is in unicellular organisms like amoeba that a single cell performs all functions. In multicellular organisms like plants and animals different groups of cells perform different functions, and this forms tissues and a division of labour.
s: Amoeba: one cell does all functions
Multicellular: groups of cells share functions

questions.q: Kabir says, 'Animals are always mobile, and since animal cells lack a rigid wall they can change shape.' Judge each part of his statement.
questions.a: Partly right. The second part is right: without a rigid cell wall animal cells change shape easily, which suits locomotion. The first part is wrong: animals can move in general, but some, such as sponges, are immobile.
s: Second part correct: no rigid wall, shape change
First part wrong: sponges are immobile

questions.q: Show that an organ cannot exist in a body that has no tissues. Use the chapter's hierarchy.
questions.a: An organ is formed when more than one type of tissue comes together. A tissue is itself a group of similar cells with a function. If there were no tissues, there would be nothing to combine, so organs, and then organ systems, could not form.
s: Organ formed from more than one type of tissue
Tissue is the level below organ

questions.q: Compare a banyan tree and a goat on three points: how they get their food, whether they stay fixed or move, and what the cells' wall allows. For each point name one tissue-related consequence the chapter gives, and conclude why the two have different tissues.
questions.a: Nutrition: the plant has tissues to use solar energy for photosynthesis; the goat has tissues to digest food from external sources. Mobility: the banyan is fixed and needs support; the goat moves. Cell wall: banyan cells have a rigid wall for strength and shape; goat cells lack one and change shape easily, suiting locomotion. Because their ways of life differ, their growth, transport and other tissues differ, e.g. xylem in plants and muscle tissue in animals.
s: Cell wall contrast and what it allows
Conclusion: different ways of life give different tissues

questions.q: Design a poster titled 'From one cell to a whole person'. Name the five levels in order, give one example of your own for each level (use the heart or the stomach), and explain in two sentences how division of labour helps the person.
questions.a: Levels: cell, tissue, organ, organ system, organism. Example for the heart: a cardiac muscle cell; a group of similar cardiac muscle cells forming cardiac muscle tissue; the heart as an organ made of more than one tissue type; the circulatory system of heart and blood vessels; the person. Division of labour: different tissues do different jobs such as movement, control and protection, so the body works more efficiently and can carry out complex life processes.
s: Five levels in the correct order
A fitting example at each level

questions.q:
During a visit to a college lab in Mysuru, Class 9 students look at four specimens: (P) a drop of pond water holding an amoeba, (Q) a thin slice of a mango leaf, (R) a smear of cells from the inside of a goat's cheek and (S) a wall chart of a sponge, an animal that stays fixed to a rock.
(a) Which specimen shows a whole organism in which a single cell does all life functions, and what name does the chapter use for such organisms?
(b) Which of Q and R would you expect to have cells with a rigid wall, and why does that suit its way of life?
(c) Does the sponge in S contradict what the chapter says about animals and movement? Explain.
(d) Time allows only one more slide: a second leaf slice or a second cheek smear. Choose one and say what it adds to the contrast between plant and animal tissue.
questions.a: (a) P; such organisms are unicellular. (b) Q, the leaf: plants are mostly fixed and need support, and the rigid wall gives strength and a fixed shape. (c) No, the chapter says animals can move in general, although some such as sponges are immobile. (d) Either is acceptable if justified: a second cheek smear shows more animal cells changing shape without a rigid wall; a second leaf slice shows more rigid-walled cells; either adds to the contrast of wall and shape.
s: (b) leaf Q, fixed organism needs support
(c) no contradiction, sponges noted as immobile exception
(d) a justified choice linked to wall and shape

questions.q:
A school debate compares a mango tree and a buffalo. The table kept by the judges reads: Mobility: tree fixed, buffalo moves. Cell wall: tree cells rigid wall, buffalo cells none. Food: tree makes food using sunlight, buffalo takes in food and digests it. The speakers must say which design needs which tissue.
(a) Which entry in the table explains why the buffalo has tissues for digestion and the tree has tissues for photosynthesis?
(b) Which two entries together explain why the buffalo's body is suited to locomotion?
(c) Name one tissue each that the chapter gives for the tree and the buffalo as examples of specialisation for their way of life.
(d) One judge says, 'A tree needs more tissues than a buffalo, so a tree is more advanced.' Is the data enough to say this? Justify.
questions.a: (a) The food row: sunlight versus digestion of external food. (b) Mobility (it moves) and cell wall (none, so cells change shape easily). (c) Tree: xylem (or phloem) for transport; buffalo: muscle tissue (or nervous tissue). (d) No, the table compares the ways of life, not the number of tissues; each organism has tissues suited to its way of life, so 'more advanced' is not supported.
s: (c) xylem or phloem; muscle or nervous tissue
(d) data show difference not rank, justified

questions.q: Two onion bulbs are set over water. On day 3 Teena snips about 1 cm off every root tip of bulb X and leaves bulb Y alone. What should she record by day 6?
questions.a: Roots of X stop lengthening while roots of Y keep growing. Roots grow in length only from their tips, where the cells divide continuously; without the tip, the root stops growing.
o: Roots of X stop lengthening while roots of Y keep growing
Roots of X lengthen faster because the cut gives their cells room to divide
Roots of both X and Y keep lengthening from their bases
Roots of Y stop lengthening because nothing has been cut off them

questions.q: A felled tree trunk shows 36 rings. Rings 10 and 11 are very narrow, while ring 20 is very wide. Which inference does the chapter support?
questions.a: The tree was about 36 years old, and growth conditions were poor in years 10 and 11 and favourable in year 20. Annual rings are counted to estimate age, and wide and narrow rings reflect favourable or unfavourable growth conditions.
o: The tree was about 36 years old, and growth conditions were poor in years 10 and 11 and favourable in year 20
The tree was about 36 months old, and the narrow rings mark the months when it stopped living
The tree was 36 years old, and rings 10 and 11 show the lateral meristem was missing then
The tree was about 36 years old, and ring width tells nothing about conditions in a year

questions.q: A gardener trims the top 10 cm off a hedge. Two weeks later it looks bushy, with new shoots coming from lower down the stems. Which tissue is mainly responsible for the new shoots?
questions.a: Intercalary meristem at the nodes. When the tip is cut, the stem stops lengthening, but new branches arise from the nodes where intercalary meristem is present.
o: Intercalary meristem at the nodes
Apical meristem at the cut tips
Lateral meristem in the ring of the stem
Sclerenchyma of the stem

questions.q: Under a microscope Farid sees four groups of cells. Which group is most likely to be meristematic tissue?
questions.a: Small cells, thin walls, big nucleus, dense cytoplasm, no vacuole, tightly packed together. Meristematic cells divide continuously and are small, thin walled, with a large nucleus, dense cytoplasm, little or no vacuole and tight packing.
o: Small cells, thin walls, big nucleus, dense cytoplasm, no vacuole, tightly packed together
Large cells with a big central vacuole, thin walls, and loose packing with air gaps between them
Elongated cells with thick lignified walls, mostly dead, with narrow cavities inside them
Large rectangular cells in one flat layer covered by a thin waxy coating on top of them

questions.q:
Read three statements about plant growth.
Statement 1: Lateral meristem is a ring of dividing cells that adds new cells inside and outside, so the stem becomes thicker.
Statement 2: If the tip of a young stem is cut, the stem goes on growing in length from the cut surface.
Statement 3: Intercalary meristem lies at the base of an internode or just above a node.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 3 only. After the tip is cut the stem stops growing in length, so statement 2 is false; statements 1 and 3 are correct.
o: 1 and 3 only
2 only
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): A root whose tip has been cut off stops growing in length.
Reason (R): The root tip holds actively dividing cells, and new length is added only from there.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Both are true, and the dividing cells of the tip are the reason the root lengthens, so the loss of the tip stops growth.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match each observation (Column I) with the idea it shows (Column II).
Column I: 1. A lawn grows back after mowing  2. Cells made at a root tip stop dividing and become storage cells  3. A trunk gets thicker each year  4. A sapling's shoot tip adds 3 cm in a week
Column II: a. Lateral meristem  b. Apical meristem  c. Intercalary meristem  d. Differentiation
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b. Grass regrows through intercalary meristem; cells that lose the ability to divide and specialise show differentiation; girth comes from lateral meristem; shoot tip lengthening comes from apical meristem.

questions.q: A trunk cut for timber shows 18 wide rings and 27 narrow rings. Counting all rings, its age is estimated as ___ years.

Two onion roots are measured: Jar A 1.0, 2.0, 3.2, 4.1, 5.2, 6.0 cm on days 1 to 6. Jar B matches Jar A to day 3 (3.2 cm), then its tip is cut and it reads 3.2 cm on days 4, 5 and 6.
(a) How much did each root lengthen from day 3 to day 6?
(b) Explain the difference using the chapter.
questions.a: (a) Jar A: 6.0 - 3.2 = 2.8 cm; Jar B: 0 cm. (b) Roots grow only from their tips, which hold actively dividing cells; Jar B lost its tip, so it stopped lengthening.
s: (b) growth only from tip with dividing cells

questions.q:
A stem has one node at 12 cm and the next node at 31 cm from its base.
(a) What is the length of the internode between them?
(b) Where along this internode would the intercalary meristem be found?
questions.a: (a) 31 - 12 = 19 cm. (b) At the base of the internode, just above the lower node.
s: (b) base of the internode, just above the node

questions.q:
Of 100 new cells formed at a root tip in a day, 60 lose the ability to divide.
(a) What happens to these 60 cells, and what is the process called?
(b) What do the other 40 cells keep doing?
questions.a: (a) They change in structure and function and become specialised permanent tissue; the process is differentiation. (b) They remain meristematic and keep dividing, adding new cells.
s: (a) become specialised permanent tissue by differentiation

questions.q: Differentiate apical meristem from lateral meristem on two points: where it lies and what kind of growth it brings.
questions.a: Apical meristem lies at the tips of roots and shoots and increases length. Lateral meristem is a ring of dividing cells along the circumference of the stem and increases girth.

questions.q:
A tree's tip is cut by a storm.
(a) Does the stem go on growing in length from the cut tip?
(b) Where do new branches then arise, and from which meristem?
questions.a: (a) No, the stem stops growing in length. (b) New branches arise from the nodes, through intercalary meristem.
s: (a) no further lengthening from the cut

questions.q: True or False: A wide annual ring in a trunk shows that the tree had favourable growth conditions in that year. Give the reason.
questions.a: True. Annual rings differ in width because of favourable or unfavourable growth conditions in a particular year, so a wide ring marks a favourable year.
s: Reason: ring width reflects the year's growth conditions

questions.q: True or False: Lateral meristem sits at the tip of a stem, which is why stems grow in girth. Give the reason or correct it.
questions.a: False. Lateral meristem is a ring of actively dividing cells along the circumference of the stem; tips hold the apical meristem, which increases length.
s: Correction: ring along the stem adds girth, tip meristem adds length

questions.q: Mira says, 'Cutting the root tip of a seedling stops its root from lengthening, because the tip has the actively dividing cells.' Is she correct?
questions.a: Yes. The onion-root activity showed that the root whose tip was cut stopped growing while the intact one grew, so roots lengthen only from their tips, where cells divide continuously.
s: Evidence: cut-tip root stopped, intact kept growing

questions.q: Dev says, 'Counting the rings of a tree trunk gives its age, but the ring widths tell us nothing about the weather.' Judge his statement.
questions.a: Partly right. Counting annual rings does estimate the age of the tree. But wide and narrow rings reflect favourable or unfavourable conditions, so scientists can also understand the climatic conditions in which it grew.

questions.q: Write a field situation that can be explained only by intercalary meristem, and show why neither apical nor lateral meristem explains it.
questions.a: E.g. a lawn mowed down regrows within days. The tips were removed, so apical meristem cannot explain regrowth; the stem did not get thicker, so lateral meristem is not the cause. Intercalary meristem at the nodes regenerates the plant after cutting.
s: A valid cutting or grazing situation
Why apical and lateral meristem do not fit

questions.q: Design a fair test to show that roots grow in length only from their tips. Name what you will vary, three things kept the same, what you will measure and on which days, and the result you expect.
questions.a: Two onion bulbs of similar size in two jars with equal water, same light and temperature. Vary only the tip: in one jar cut about 1 cm from the root tips on day 3, leave the other intact. Measure root length daily. Expect the intact roots to keep lengthening and the cut roots to stop; conclusion: growth is from dividing cells at the tips.
s: Single variable: tips cut or not
Conclusion about tips and dividing cells

questions.q: A teak tree's trunk diameter was 6, 14, 22, 30 and 34 cm at ages 8, 16, 24, 32 and 40 years. Work out the yearly girth increase in each 8-year interval, describe the trend, name the tissue behind the increase and say where it lies, and say how the rings would show the trend.
questions.a: Increases: 8, 8, 8, 4 cm over 8 years each, i.e. 1.0, 1.0, 1.0 and 0.5 cm per year. The tree thickened steadily and then slowed after age 32. The lateral meristem, a ring of dividing cells in the stem, adds cells inside and outside. The rings would be wide in the first intervals and narrower in the last.
s: Lateral meristem and its ring location

questions.q:
Two trees from a Bengaluru road-widening site are brought to a school science museum. Tree A has 62 annual rings with an average radial ring width of 3.1 mm. Tree B has 38 annual rings with an average radial ring width of 5.2 mm. The museum can keep only one cross-section to teach climate and age.
(a) Estimate the age of each tree.
(b) Work out the radius and the diameter, in cm, of each trunk to 1 decimal place, and say which is thicker.
(c) Which tissue produced the girth of both trees, and where does it lie?
(d) Which section would you keep, and what does the other offer that you give up?
questions.a: (a) Tree A about 62 years; Tree B about 38 years. (b) A: 62 x 3.1 = 192.2 mm, radius 19.2 cm, diameter 38.4 cm; B: 38 x 5.2 = 197.6 mm, radius 19.8 cm, diameter 39.5 cm; B is slightly thicker though far younger. (c) Lateral meristem, a ring of dividing cells in the stem. (d) Either, justified: A gives a longer record of years and conditions; B shows faster growth in a more favourable period. Size alone does not give age.
s: (b) diameters 38.4 cm and 39.5 cm, B thicker

questions.q:
A school nursery in Pune prunes the top 15 cm of every sapling of a hedge plant. A teacher records that after 20 days the main stem has not become taller, but 4 to 6 new branches have appeared per plant, all from points on the stem where leaves had been attached. Roots under a few pots, checked at the same time, are 2 cm longer than at pruning.
(a) What is the name of the points from which the branches appeared, and which meristem is at work there?
(b) Why did the main stem not become taller?
(c) Which meristem lengthened the roots, and where is it?
(d) The nursery wants a taller single-stemmed plant for a ceremony. Should it prune or not? Justify using your answers.
questions.a: (a) Nodes; intercalary meristem. (b) The apical meristem at the shoot tip was removed, so the stem stops growing in length. (c) Apical meristem at the root tips. (d) Do not prune: pruning removes the shoot tip and makes the plant bushy with branches rather than taller; leave the apical meristem intact for height. Pruning is right if a bushy hedge is wanted.
s: (c) root apical meristem at the tips

questions.q: Bhavna bends a fresh hibiscus twig and a tendril of a pea plant; neither snaps. Which tissue and cell feature explain this?
questions.a: Collenchyma, living cells with unevenly thickened corners. Collenchyma gives support with flexibility because of pectin deposits at its corners, so stems and tendrils bend without breaking.
o: Collenchyma, living cells with unevenly thickened corners
Sclerenchyma, whose cells have thick lignified walls and are mostly dead
Parenchyma, whose cells are thin walled and loosely packed with spaces
Xylem, whose vessels are tubular, thick walled and carry water upward

questions.q: A cut balsam stem is stood in red ink. After some hours red lines appear along the stem. Which tissue carried the ink up, and what does it normally carry?
questions.a: Xylem, carrying water and minerals up from roots. Xylem transports water and minerals from the roots to other parts, so coloured water rises in it.
o: Xylem, carrying water and minerals up from roots
Phloem, which carries food made in the leaves to other parts
Epidermis, which carries water from the roots to the leaf tips
Parenchyma, which carries food from the roots to the green leaves

questions.q: A pond plant has big air-filled spaces in its stem, and the stem floats at the surface. In green parts the same tissue also makes food. Which tissue is it?
questions.a: Parenchyma, forming air spaces for floating. Parenchyma is living, thin walled, loosely packed with spaces; in aquatic plants it forms air spaces for floating and in green parts does photosynthesis.
o: Parenchyma, forming air spaces for floating
Collenchyma, whose corners are thickened by pectin deposits
Sclerenchyma, whose walls are thick with deposited lignin
Companion cells of the phloem beside the sieve tubes

questions.q: A student claims that every cell in xylem is dead. Which cell of xylem proves him wrong?
questions.a: Xylem parenchyma, the one living component. Tracheids, vessels and xylem fibres are primarily sclerenchymatous, but xylem parenchyma is living.
o: Xylem parenchyma, the one living component
Tracheid, a tubular thick walled cell of the xylem
Vessel, a tubular thick walled cell of the xylem
Xylem fibre, a sclerenchymatous cell of the xylem

questions.q:
Read three statements.
Statement 1: The epidermis is loosely packed, with large air spaces between its cells.
Statement 2: Root hair, which arise from epidermal cells, increase the surface area for absorbing water and minerals.
Statement 3: Sieve tubes are dead cells that carry water upward from the roots.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 2 only. The epidermis is tightly packed and sieve tubes carry food, so statements 1 and 3 are wrong; statement 2 is correct.
o: 2 only
1 only
1 and 3 only
1, 2 and 3

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The epidermis of a leaf has pores called stomata.
Reason (R): The cells of the epidermis are covered with a waxy layer of cutin called the cuticle.
questions.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both statements are true, but the cuticle does not explain why pores are present; stomata serve gaseous exchange and transpiration.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match each situation (Column I) with the tissue responsible (Column II).
Column I: 1. A coconut husk mat stays tough  2. A pea tendril bends without breaking  3. A lotus stalk has air spaces that help it float  4. Sugar made in a leaf reaches a growing root tip
Column II: a. Phloem  b. Collenchyma  c. Parenchyma  d. Sclerenchyma
questions.a: 1-d, 2-b, 3-c, 4-a. Husk fibres are sclerenchyma, tendrils bend due to collenchyma, floating needs parenchyma air spaces, and food moves through phloem.

questions.q: A gardener smears wax on the underside of a leaf and blocks its pores. The pores that can no longer exchange gases are called ___.
questions.a: stomata

questions.q:
(a) The epidermis of a leaf has pores. Name them and state two jobs they do.
(b) The epidermis of a root grows hair-like projections. Name them and state what they gain the plant.
questions.a: (a) Stomata; they help in gaseous exchange and in transpiration. (b) Root hair; they increase the surface area for absorbing water and minerals from the soil.
s: (b) root hair and larger absorbing surface

questions.q:
A phloem cell is long and tubular, joined end to end to the next by perforated walls.
(a) Name this cell and say what it carries.
(b) Name the neighbouring cell that monitors loading and unloading of sugars in it.
questions.a: (a) Sieve tube cell; it transports food from the leaves to other parts of the plant. (b) Companion cell, a specialised parenchyma cell that regulates the sieve tube cells.

questions.q: Differentiate simple permanent tissue from complex permanent tissue, giving one example of each.
questions.a: Simple permanent tissue is made of only one type of cell, e.g. parenchyma; complex permanent tissue is made of more than one type of cell working together, e.g. xylem.
s: Simple: one cell type with example
Complex: more than one cell type with example

questions.q: A walnut shell is hard but a lettuce leaf stalk is soft. Using cell features, give one reason each for the hardness of a seed covering and the softness of a parenchyma-rich tissue.
questions.a: Seed coverings and shells contain sclerenchyma, whose thick lignified walls make it hard and strong. Parenchyma has thin walls and is loosely packed with intercellular spaces, so it is soft.

questions.q:
(a) Place epidermis, collenchyma and phloem under the dermal, ground and vascular tissue systems.
(b) Which of the three systems contains only complex tissues?
questions.a: (a) Epidermis: dermal; collenchyma: ground; phloem: vascular. (b) The vascular tissue system, made of xylem and phloem.

questions.q: True or False: Parenchyma and collenchyma consist of living cells, but sclerenchyma is mostly dead. Give the reason.
questions.a: True. Parenchyma has living thin-walled cells and collenchyma has living cells with thickened corners; sclerenchyma cells have thick lignified walls and most of them are dead.
s: Reason: living thin and corner-thickened cells, mostly dead lignified sclerenchyma

questions.q: Priya says, 'Xylem consists only of dead cells, so no living cell takes part in carrying water.' Is she correct?
questions.a: No. Tracheids, vessels and xylem fibres are primarily sclerenchymatous, but xylem parenchyma is a living component of xylem. So xylem is not made only of dead cells.

questions.q: Imran says, 'Xylem carries water and minerals from the roots, and it also gives the plant strength.' Is he correct?
questions.a: Yes. Xylem transports water and minerals from the roots to other parts, and the chapter says it also provides strength to the plant, helped by its thick-walled tracheids, vessels and fibres.

questions.q: Show that a tendril made only of sclerenchyma could not bend without breaking.
questions.a: Sclerenchyma cells have thick lignified walls and are hard and strong, and most are dead. Bending needs flexibility, which collenchyma gives through its thickened corners. A tendril of sclerenchyma alone would be rigid, so it would snap instead of bending.

questions.q: Compare xylem and phloem on five points: what each carries and in which direction, which cells make it up, which cell is living in each, how each gets its strength, and the cell that regulates the transporting tubes.
questions.a: Xylem carries water and minerals from the roots to other parts; phloem carries food from the leaves to other parts. Xylem has tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres; phloem has sieve tubes, companion cells, phloem parenchyma and phloem fibres. In xylem only the parenchyma is living; phloem is mostly living. Strength comes from fibres and thick walls in xylem, and phloem fibres in phloem. Companion cells regulate sieve tubes in phloem.

questions.q: A sunflower stem section shows epidermis, parenchyma, collenchyma, sclerenchyma, xylem and phloem. For each, say whether it is simple or complex, give its main job and name its tissue system.
questions.a: Epidermis: protective, dermal system (a single layer, simple in cell type). Parenchyma: simple, stores food and photosynthesises, ground system. Collenchyma: simple, flexible support, ground system. Sclerenchyma: simple, hard strong support, ground system. Xylem: complex, conducts water and minerals, vascular system. Phloem: complex, conducts food, vascular system.

questions.q:
A lab report on three stem sections reads: Section P has living cells with corners thickened unevenly by pectin. Section Q has thick lignified walls and mostly dead cells. Section R has living, thin-walled cells, loosely packed with gaps, and some of them are green. A craft school in Kerala wants to make a doormat and must choose a material.
(a) Identify P, Q and R.
(b) Which section would form the hard coat of a walnut?
(c) Which section would store food and carry out photosynthesis?
(d) The mat must be tough, but the craft head also wants it to flex when rolled. Which section type would you pick, and what trade-off do you accept?
questions.a: (a) P collenchyma, Q sclerenchyma, R parenchyma. (b) Q, sclerenchyma. (c) R, parenchyma. (d) Q for toughness, as with coconut husk, accepting low flexibility; or P for flexibility, accepting less hardness. A justified choice earns the mark.

questions.q:
Two leafy twigs of the same plant are placed in red ink for 3 hours. Twig A is untouched and the ink climbs 12 cm. In twig B the leaves are coated with wax over their pores, and the ink climbs 4 cm.
(a) Work out the speed of the ink rise in each twig in cm per hour.
(b) Which tissue carried the ink, and what does it normally carry?
(c) Explain the difference using the epidermal structure and process the chapter links to water movement.
(d) A farmer proposes waxing the leaves of his plants during a dry spell. Judge this using your answers.
questions.a: (a) A: 12/3 = 4 cm per hour; B: 4/3 = 1.3 cm per hour. (b) Xylem; water and minerals. (c) Stomata allow transpiration, which creates a pull in xylem; waxing blocked the stomata, so the rise slowed by about 67%. (d) Waxing cuts water loss and water movement, but it also blocks gaseous exchange and slows the water pull and removal of wastes, so the plant is harmed unless only limited cover is used.

questions.q: A slide of the lining of a child's small intestine, which takes up digested nutrients, is shown. Which description is the likeliest for what the student sees?
questions.a: A single layer of tall pillar-like cells, often hair-like. Absorption epithelium is a single layer of tall pillar-like cells, often with hair-like structures, as in the lining of the small intestine.
o: A single layer of tall pillar-like cells, often hair-like
A single layer of thin, flat cells that allow quick diffusion
Many layers of cells whose outer cells are flat and tightly packed
Specialised receptor cells carrying hair-like cilia on top

questions.q: A footballer's knee is twisted so far that the joint nearly slips out of place before the joint stops. Which tissue normally limits such movement, and what does it join?
questions.a: Ligament, which joins bone to bone. Ligaments connect bone to bone, give stability, limit movement and help prevent dislocation.
o: Ligament, which joins bone to bone
Tendon, which joins muscle to bone
Cartilage, which cushions the ends of bones
Bone, which has a rigid matrix of calcium and phosphorus compounds

questions.q: An adult has 5 litres of blood. Using the proportions in the chapter, how much of it is plasma?
questions.a: 2.75 litres. Plasma is 55% of the total volume: 0.55 x 5 = 2.75 litres, while formed elements are the remaining 2.25 litres.
o: 2.75 litres
2.25 litres
0.55 litre
4.5 litres

questions.q: Mohan gets a cut that bleeds and then clots. A week later a different scrape turns red, swollen and filled with pus. Which pairing of blood component and observation is correct?
questions.a: Platelets for the clot, white blood cells for the redness, swelling and pus. Platelets help in clotting at an injury; white blood cells collect at infected areas, causing pus and inflammation.
o: Platelets for the clot, white blood cells for the redness, swelling and pus
Red blood cells for the clot, platelets for the redness, swelling and the pus
White blood cells for the clot, plasma for the redness, swelling and the pus
Platelets for the clot, and the same platelets for redness, swelling and pus

questions.q:
Read three statements.
Statement 1: Bone has a rigid matrix containing calcium and phosphorus compounds.
Statement 2: Cartilage cushions the ends of bones, acting as a shock absorber.
Statement 3: Tendons join bone to bone and prevent a joint from going beyond its limit.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1 and 2 only. Tendons connect muscle to bone, not bone to bone, so statement 3 is false.
o: 1 and 2 only
3 only
1 and 3 only
2 and 3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The epithelium of the skin is a single layer of thin flat cells that allows rapid diffusion of gases.
Reason (R): The epithelium of the skin has many layers and protects underlying tissues from injury, friction and entry of microbes.
questions.a: A is false but R is true. A is false because skin epithelium has many layers and is protective, while rapid-diffusion epithelium is the single thin layer in lungs and blood vessels; R is true.
o: A is false but R is true
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false

questions.q:
Match each experience (Column I) with the connective tissue it points to (Column II).
Column I: 1. Wiggle fingers and feel the forearm move  2. Fold your ear and it springs back  3. Raise your leg and the knee stops at a limit  4. Touch the elbow and feel a hard, rigid structure
Column II: a. Ligament  b. Bone  c. Cartilage  d. Tendon
questions.a: 1-d, 2-c, 3-a, 4-b. A tendon links muscle to bone, cartilage is soft and flexible, a ligament limits joint movement, and bone is hard and rigid.

questions.q: A donor gives 400 mL of blood. Plasma is 55% of blood by volume, so the plasma in the donation is about ___ mL.

(a) How does the structure of the epithelium lining blood vessels differ from that of skin?
(b) Use your answer to (a) to explain why each structure suits its job.
questions.a: (a) The lining of blood vessels is a single layer of thin flat cells; skin epithelium has many layers with flat, tightly packed outer cells. (b) The thin single layer lets liquids and gases diffuse rapidly; the many layers protect underlying tissues from injury, friction and microbes.
s: (a) single thin layer versus many layers

questions.q:
A red blood cell lives for about 4 months.
(a) How many successive red cells replace one lineage over 24 months?
(b) What iron-rich protein makes blood red?
questions.a: (a) 24 / 4 = about 6 red blood cells in succession, since they are replaced regularly. (b) Haemoglobin, found in the red blood cells.

questions.q: Differentiate tendon from ligament on what each connects and what it does for a joint.
questions.a: A tendon connects muscle to bone and brings about movement; a ligament connects bone to bone and gives stability, limits movement and helps prevent dislocation.
s: Ligament: bone to bone, stability and limit

questions.q:
Blood and bone are both connective tissues.
(a) What property of their matrix makes one fluid and the other hard?
(b) Name the substances that make the bone matrix rigid.
questions.a: (a) Blood's matrix is watery, soft and jelly-like; bone's matrix is hard, solid and rigid. (b) Compounds of calcium and phosphorus.
s: (a) matrix soft and watery versus hard and rigid

questions.q:
The lining of the nostrils, the taste buds and the inner ear carry the same kind of epithelium.
(a) What cells and feature does it have?
(b) What do the three sites have in common that explains this?
questions.a: (a) Specialised receptor cells having hair-like cilia. (b) All three sense things: smell, taste, and sound and balance.

questions.q: True or False: Tendons connect bone to bone and prevent dislocation of a joint. Give the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. Tendons connect muscle to bone and bring about movement; ligaments are the tissue that connects bone to bone and helps prevent dislocation.
s: Correction: tendon is muscle to bone, ligament bone to bone

questions.q: Neha says, 'Blood and bone look nothing alike, yet both are connective tissues because both connect and support, and they differ in matrix.' Is she right?
questions.a: Yes. A tissue that connects and supports other tissues is connective tissue. Blood connects parts by transporting nutrients, gases and hormones, and bone supports the body. They differ in matrix: watery, soft and jelly-like in blood and hard and rigid in bone.

questions.q: Ravi says, 'Platelets are the blood cells that gather at an infected spot and cause pus.' Is he right?
questions.a: No. White blood cells collect at infected areas, causing pus formation and inflammation. Platelets help clotting at the site of an injury.

questions.q: Show that the epithelium lining the air sacs of the lungs cannot be a thick, many-layered protective type without hurting its job.
questions.a: Lungs need rapid diffusion of gases across the lining, which a single layer of thin, flat cells allows. A many-layered type is built for protection against injury, friction and microbes, and would slow diffusion across it.
s: Single thin flat layer allows it
Many layers suit protection, slow exchange

questions.q: For five sites (lining of a blood vessel, skin, sweat gland, taste bud, small intestine), name the epithelial function, describe the structure and explain in one line why it suits the job.
questions.a: Blood vessel: exchange, single layer of thin flat cells, rapid diffusion. Skin: protection, many layers with flat tightly packed outer cells, resists injury and microbes. Sweat gland: secretion, cuboidal or columnar cells specialised to produce and release substances. Taste bud: sensory, receptor cells with hair-like cilia to sense taste. Small intestine: absorption, single layer of tall pillar-like cells, often with hair-like structure, for efficient uptake.

questions.q: Link three daily experiences to blood components: a small cut that bleeds then stops, a skin infection that turns red and swollen, and running that makes breathing faster and the face red. Name the component or process for each and explain.
questions.a: Cut: platelets help the blood clot at the injury. Infection: white blood cells collect at the infected area, causing pus, redness and swelling. Running: muscles need more oxygen, so breathing becomes faster and blood flow increases, making the face appear red. Red colour of blood itself is due to haemoglobin in red blood cells.
s: White blood cells at the infection
Oxygen need with faster breathing and blood flow

questions.q:
A blood donation camp in Nagpur collects 20 donations of 400 mL each. The staff separate each donation into plasma (55% of volume) and formed elements (45%). Cold storage can hold only the plasma portion or only the formed-elements portion for the next 24 hours. Patient P is bleeding and her blood is not clotting well. Patient Q has been infected, with a red swollen wound and pus.
(a) How many litres of plasma and of formed elements do the 20 donations give?
(b) Which formed element helps clotting, and which collects at an infected site?
(c) Name the iron-rich protein in red blood cells that colours blood and give the lifespan of these cells.
(d) The camp must store only one portion. Which would you keep and what would you give up?
questions.a: (a) Plasma 20 x 220 mL = 4.4 L; formed elements 20 x 180 mL = 3.6 L. (b) Platelets help clotting; white blood cells collect at infected areas. (c) Haemoglobin; about 4 months. (d) Either with reasons: formed elements hold platelets for P and white cells for Q, while plasma is the larger volume carrying the other substances; the choice gives up one portion's benefits.

questions.q:
A scan report of a runner's knee reads: tendon intact, ligament torn, cartilage intact, bone not fractured. The runner is eager to play in a match in two days.
(a) Which tissue still carries the pull of the muscle to the bone, and what does it connect?
(b) Which job of the damaged tissue is lost, and what could happen at the joint?
(c) Which tissue still cushions the ends of the bones?
(d) Advise the runner on playing, using your answers, and say what would be risked.
questions.a: (a) Tendon; it connects muscle to bone. (b) The ligament, which connects bone to bone, gives stability, limits movement and helps prevent dislocation, so the knee may go beyond its limit or dislocate. (c) Cartilage. (d) Do not play: though muscle pull, cushioning and bone are fine, the joint has lost its stability and could dislocate; playing risks a worse injury.

questions.q: A slide from a sprinter's thigh shows long cylindrical fibres that do not branch, have many nuclei each and show light and dark bands. Which muscle type is it and what movement does it serve?
questions.a: Skeletal muscle, which serves voluntary movement. Unbranched, multinucleate, striated fibres attached to the skeleton are skeletal muscle, which brings about voluntary movements such as running.
o: Skeletal muscle, which serves voluntary movement
Cardiac muscle, which serves involuntary movement
Smooth muscle, which serves slow continuous movement
Skeletal muscle, which serves involuntary movement

questions.q: A message reaches a neuron from the fingertip and leaves it towards the muscles of the forearm. Which pairing correctly gives the part that receives the signal and the part that carries the message away from the cell body?
questions.a: Dendrites receive; the axon carries the message away. Dendrites receive signals from other neurons; the axon is the long fibre that carries messages from the cell body and ends at axon terminals.
o: Dendrites receive; the axon carries the message away
The axon receives; the dendrites carry the message away
The cell body receives; the dendrites carry the message away
Dendrites receive; the cell body carries the message to the terminals

questions.q: Anita says, 'I decide when to eat, so I also control the movement of food through my intestine.' Which reply fits the chapter?
questions.a: Food moves along the intestine by involuntary smooth muscle, slow and continuous, not under conscious control. Movement of food in the intestine is involuntary and carried out by smooth muscle.
o: Food moves along the intestine by involuntary smooth muscle, slow and continuous, not under conscious control
Food moves along the intestine by skeletal muscle, which is attached to the skeleton and so is voluntary
Food moves because cardiac muscle in the intestinal wall beats rhythmically on command
Food moves under conscious control because every muscle obeys the person's will

questions.q: Which of the following activities is NOT carried out by skeletal muscle?
questions.a: The beating of the heart. Writing, lifting and running are voluntary movements by skeletal muscles; the heartbeat is involuntary and is done by cardiac muscle.
o: The beating of the heart
Writing in a notebook
Lifting a school bag
Running across a field

questions.q:
Read three statements.
Statement 1: Cardiac muscle is found in the walls of the stomach and intestine.
Statement 2: Dendrites carry messages away from the cell body to other cells.
Statement 3: Nervous tissue forms the body's control and coordination network.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 3 only. Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart, and dendrites receive signals; only statement 3 is correct.
o: 3 only
1 only
2 and 3 only
1 and 2 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): Muscles, voluntary and involuntary, cannot work on their own.
Reason (R): Muscles receive instructions from the nervous tissue.
questions.a: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A. Both are true, and the instructions from nervous tissue are why muscles cannot function independently; e.g. the brain signals the heart to beat faster during exercise.
o: Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match each activity (Column I) with the tissue involved (Column II).
Column I: 1. The heart beating through the night without tiring  2. A student writing notes  3. Food pushed slowly along the intestine  4. A hand pulled away from a hot pan
Column II: a. Skeletal muscle  b. Nervous tissue  c. Smooth muscle  d. Cardiac muscle
questions.a: 1-d, 2-a, 3-c, 4-b. Cardiac muscle beats without fatigue, skeletal muscle writes, smooth muscle moves food slowly, and nervous tissue controls the quick withdrawal.

questions.q: A slide has 40 muscle cells: 15 are unbranched with many nuclei, and the other 25 are spindle-shaped or branched with a single nucleus. The percentage of cells of the involuntary kind is ___ %.

(a) Give two differences between skeletal muscle fibres and cardiac muscle fibres in structure.
(b) Which of the two can a person move at will?
questions.a: (a) Skeletal fibres are unbranched, multinucleate and clearly striated; cardiac fibres are branched, with a single nucleus and faint striations. (b) Skeletal muscle, which carries out voluntary movements.

questions.q:
A slide of 60 muscle cells has 24 long unbranched multinucleate cells, 12 cylindrical branched single-nucleus cells with faint stripes and 24 spindle-shaped single-nucleus cells with no stripes.
(a) Name the three groups.
(b) What percentage of the cells belongs to involuntary muscle?
questions.a: (a) Skeletal, cardiac and smooth muscle. (b) (12 + 24) / 60 x 100 = 60%.

questions.q: Differentiate voluntary from involuntary movement, giving one movement and the muscle type for each.
questions.a: Voluntary movements are under conscious control, e.g. running, done by skeletal muscle. Involuntary movements happen automatically, e.g. the beating of the heart by cardiac muscle or movement of food by smooth muscle.

questions.q:
A cricketer's heart beats faster as he sprints between wickets.
(a) Which tissue instructs the heart?
(b) Why is the muscle of the heart called involuntary?
questions.a: (a) Nervous tissue, with the brain as the control centre. (b) It works automatically and rhythmically without conscious control throughout life.

questions.q: Name the part of a neuron that (a) contains the nucleus and controls the cell's activities, and (b) passes the message on to other cells.
questions.a: (a) The cell body. (b) The axon terminals at the end of the axon.

questions.q: True or False: When a player sprints, her muscles act on their own, with no instructions from nervous tissue. Give the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. Muscles, voluntary and involuntary, cannot function independently; they receive instructions from nervous tissue, as when the brain signals the heart to beat faster during exercise.
s: Correction: muscles receive instructions from nervous tissue

questions.q: True or False: Cardiac muscle is found only in the heart, and its fibres are branched with a single nucleus. Give the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says cardiac muscle is found only in the heart, with cylindrical, branched fibres, a single nucleus and faint striations.
s: Reason: heart-only, branched fibres with one nucleus

questions.q: Karan says, 'Smooth muscle cells are striped like skeletal muscle and have many nuclei.' Is he right?
questions.a: No. Smooth muscle cells are spindle-shaped with a single nucleus and lack striations. It is skeletal muscle that is striated and multinucleate.
s: Smooth: spindle, single nucleus, no stripes
Skeletal has stripes and many nuclei

questions.q: Leela says, 'Cardiac and skeletal muscle both show striations and both have branched fibres.' Judge her statement.
questions.a: Partly right. Both show striations, though cardiac striations are faint. But only cardiac fibres are branched; skeletal fibres are unbranched.

questions.q: Write a situation in which nervous tissue, skeletal muscle and involuntary muscle are all at work, and say what each does.
questions.a: E.g. a girl runs for a bus: nervous tissue (the brain) sends instructions, skeletal muscles in the legs perform the voluntary running, and the heart's cardiac muscle beats faster under the brain's signal to meet the oxygen demand.
s: Roles of nervous tissue and skeletal muscle

questions.q: Compare skeletal, smooth and cardiac muscle on four points: cell shape and branching, number of nuclei, striations, and where found with the kind of movement.
questions.a: Skeletal: long cylindrical unbranched fibres, many nuclei, striated, attached to the skeleton, voluntary. Smooth: spindle-shaped cells, a single nucleus, no striations, in organs like stomach and intestines, slow continuous involuntary movements. Cardiac: cylindrical branched fibres, a single nucleus, faint striations, only in the heart, tireless rhythmic involuntary beating.

questions.q: Trace what happens when you pull your hand from a hot pan. Name the tissue, the neuron parts with their jobs, and the muscle that finally acts, and say why the muscle needs the tissue.
questions.a: Nervous tissue forms the control and coordination network. A neuron's dendrites receive the signal; the cell body, with the nucleus, controls the cell; the axon carries the message and its terminals pass it to other cells. Skeletal muscle then moves the hand. Muscles cannot work independently; they receive instructions from the nervous tissue, with the brain as the control centre.
s: Cell body and axon with terminals
Muscles need instructions from nervous tissue

questions.q:
During a kabaddi match in Rohtak, a player's heart beats 72 times a minute at rest and 150 times a minute in the raid. After the match the coach plans a training week with three aims: (X) quicker hand movements, (Y) a calmer digestion, (Z) a steadier heart rate, each to be trained by conscious effort.
(a) Which tissue signals the heart to beat faster, and why must it?
(b) By what percentage did the heart rate rise in the raid, to 1 decimal place?
(c) Which muscle type works the heart, and what three features describe its fibres?
(d) The coach can plan conscious training for only one aim. Which of X, Y, Z is most suited by the chapter, and why are the other two poor choices?
questions.a: (a) Nervous tissue (the brain); the body's oxygen demand rises during exercise. (b) (150 - 72) / 72 x 100 = 108.3%. (c) Cardiac muscle; fibres cylindrical, branched, with a single nucleus (and faint striations). (d) X: hand movement is voluntary, by skeletal muscle under conscious control. Digestion (smooth muscle) and the heart (cardiac muscle) are involuntary, so conscious effort is poor training for them.

questions.q:
A neurology lab studies three neurons. In neuron N1 the dendrites are damaged. In neuron N2 the axon is cut across. In neuron N3 the cell body, which holds the nucleus, is damaged. Funds allow only one neuron to be repaired in an experiment.
(a) What can N1 no longer do?
(b) What can N2 no longer do, and where would its message fail to reach?
(c) Why is damage to N3 expected to affect the whole cell?
(d) Which neuron would you repair, and what would you give up?
questions.a: (a) Receive signals from other neurons. (b) Carry the message away from the cell body to the axon terminals, so other cells would not receive it. (c) The cell body contains the nucleus and controls the cell's activities. (d) Either with reasons: N3, because the cell body controls the cell; or N1 or N2 to restore receiving or transmitting; the choice gives up the other two repairs.

questions.q: A fast bowler swings his arm forward, backward, sideways and in a full circle before releasing the ball. Which joint at the shoulder makes this possible?
questions.a: Ball and socket joint. The rounded top of the upper arm bone fits into a shallow hollow of the shoulder bone, allowing forward, backward, sideways and circular movement.
o: Ball and socket joint
Hinge joint
Pivot joint
Fixed joint

questions.q: A cyclist's knee bends and straightens in one direction only, and a small bone sits in front of it. Which joint is this, and what does the small bone do?
questions.a: A hinge joint; the kneecap protects the joint. The knee is a hinge joint like the elbow, and the kneecap protects it.
o: A hinge joint; the kneecap protects the joint
A pivot joint; the kneecap lets the leg turn from side to side
A ball and socket joint; the kneecap allows circular movement
A fixed joint; the kneecap locks the leg in position

questions.q: A 60 kg adult's skeleton makes up about 12 to 15 per cent of body weight. In what range does the skeleton's weight lie?
o: 7.2 kg to 9.0 kg
6.0 kg to 7.5 kg
12 kg to 15 kg
0.72 kg to 0.90 kg

questions.q: Which statement about joints is NOT correct?
questions.a: Joints can move the bones on their own. Joints allow movement but cannot move the bones on their own; muscles pulling through tendons do that.
o: Joints can move the bones on their own
A joint is a junction between two or more bones
Muscles are needed to move the bones at a joint
The bones of the skull are joined by fixed joints

questions.q:
Read three statements.
Statement 1: The skull is connected to the backbone by a pivot joint that lets the head move side to side.
Statement 2: A cartilage disc between vertebrae acts as a cushion and allows flexibility.
Statement 3: The ribs are joined to the sternum by flexible cartilage.
Which statements are correct?
questions.a: 1, 2 and 3. All three statements agree with the chapter.
o: 1, 2 and 3
1 and 2 only
2 and 3 only
3 only

questions.q:
Assertion (A): The rib cage can expand and contract during breathing.
Reason (R): The ribs are attached to the spine at the back and to the breastbone in front.
questions.a: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A. Both are true, but the reason does not explain the movement; the ribs are joined to the breastbone by flexible cartilage, and that flexibility allows expansion and contraction.
o: Both A and R are true but R is not the correct explanation of A
Both A and R are true and R is the correct explanation of A
A is true but R is false
A is false but R is true

questions.q:
Match each movement (Column I) with the joint that allows it (Column II).
Column I: 1. Shaking the head to say 'no'  2. Climbing a stair by bending the knee  3. Skull bones staying locked during a fall  4. Swinging the arm in a full circle
Column II: a. Fixed joint  b. Ball and socket joint  c. Pivot joint  d. Hinge joint
questions.a: 1-c, 2-d, 3-a, 4-b. Head turning is the pivot joint, the knee is a hinge, skull bones are joined by fixed joints, and the shoulder is a ball and socket.

questions.q: A 50 kg adult's skeleton is about 12 to 15 per cent of body weight, so it weighs between 6 kg and ___ kg.

A trainee weighs 80 kg.
(a) Find the range of weight of her skeleton using 12 to 15 per cent.
(b) Would a lighter trainee of 60 kg have a skeleton of the same percentage? Say what varies.
questions.a: (a) 0.12 x 80 = 9.6 kg to 0.15 x 80 = 12 kg. (b) The average share is about 12 to 15 per cent for adults, though it can vary with age, gender and body composition.
s: (b) share varies with age, gender, body composition

questions.q:
Compare the elbow with the shoulder.
(a) Which movements does each allow?
(b) Name the joint type of each.
questions.a: (a) The elbow bends and straightens in one direction only; the shoulder moves forward, backward, sideways and in circles. (b) Elbow: hinge joint; shoulder: ball and socket joint.

questions.q:
(a) What actually moves the bones at a joint, since a joint cannot move them on its own?
(b) How does the force reach the bone?
questions.a: (a) The muscles, which pull on the bones. (b) A muscle is attached to a bone by a tendon; when the muscle contracts, the tendon transmits the force to the bone, giving movement at the joint.

questions.q: A child bends forward and twists at the waist without hurting her spinal cord. Name the structure between her vertebrae that allows this and say how it helps.
questions.a: The cartilage disc between each vertebra acts as a cushion and allows flexibility, so she can bend and twist without injuring the spinal cord.
s: Cushion and flexibility protect the spinal cord

questions.q:
After a fall a boy finds breathing painful. His ribs are bruised.
(a) Which structures join his ribs to the breastbone and allow the rib cage to move?
(b) How does that movement help breathing?
questions.a: (a) Flexible cartilage. (b) The rib cage expands and contracts, increasing and decreasing the space in the chest so air moves in and out of the lungs.
s: (b) space in chest changes, air moves

questions.q: True or False: Every adult has 12 pairs of ribs, which means 24 ribs in all. Give the reason.
questions.a: True. The chapter says there are 12 pairs of ribs forming the rib cage, and 12 pairs make 12 x 2 = 24 ribs.

questions.q: True or False: Because the knee is a hinge joint like the shoulder, it allows circular movement of the leg. Give the reason or correction.
questions.a: False. The knee is a hinge joint, which bends and straightens in one direction only like a door hinge; circular movement belongs to the ball and socket joint of the shoulder.
s: Correction: hinge is one direction, ball and socket is circular

questions.q: Raj says, 'A muscle pulls on a bone through a tendon, and the tendon passes the force to the bone so the joint moves.' Is he correct?
questions.a: Yes. Muscles are attached to bones by strong, flexible bands called tendons. When a muscle contracts, the tendon transmits this force to the bone, resulting in movement at a joint.
s: Muscles attached to bones by tendons
Force transmitted, movement at the joint

questions.q: Sana says, 'The bones of the skull are joined by pivot joints so the skull can turn in every direction.' Judge her statement.
questions.a: No. The bones of the skull are joined by fixed joints and cannot move, which keeps the brain safe. The pivot joint is where the skull joins the backbone and lets the head move side to side.
s: Pivot is at skull and backbone

questions.q: Show that the elbow cannot be moved in a full circle like the shoulder.
questions.a: The elbow is a hinge joint that bends and straightens in one direction only, like a door hinge. A full circle needs a ball and socket joint, where a rounded bone end fits into a shallow hollow, so the elbow cannot give circular movement.
s: Hinge moves in one direction only
Circular movement needs ball and socket

questions.q: Compare the four types of joints in the chapter. For each give one body location, the movement allowed and the everyday picture the chapter uses.
questions.a: Ball and socket: shoulder; forward, backward, sideways and circular movement; rounded bone top in a shallow hollow. Hinge: elbow and knee; bends and straightens in one direction; like a door hinge. Pivot: skull and backbone; head moves side to side; like a doorknob turning in its socket. Fixed: skull bones; no movement; keeps the brain safe.

questions.q: Explain how a person lifts a bag of books, using the musculoskeletal system. Include the part played by muscle, tendon, bone, joint, cartilage or ligament, and the nervous system, and say what the skeleton does for the body.
questions.a: The nervous system controls the musculoskeletal system and instructs the skeletal muscle. The muscle contracts and pulls on the bone; the tendon attaches it and transmits the force, so the bone moves at the joint. Ligaments hold bones in place and limit the movement, and cartilage cushions the bone ends. The joint cannot move the bones on its own. The skeleton gives strength, supports the body and protects delicate organs.
s: Tendon transmits force, bone moves at joint

questions.q:
A cricketer in Chennai is hit on the chest. An X-ray shows his ribs are not broken, but the cartilage that joins the ribs to the breastbone is bruised and breathing is painful. The doctor also notes that the spine and skull are normal. A physio suggests strapping the chest tightly for a week so that it does not move.
(a) How many ribs does a person have in all, and which two organs do they protect?
(b) Why can bruised cartilage make breathing painful?
(c) What is the effect of tight strapping on the movement of the rib cage and on breathing?
(d) Would you accept the physio's advice? Justify.
questions.a: (a) 12 pairs, i.e. 24 ribs; heart and lungs. (b) Flexible cartilage lets the rib cage expand and contract in breathing, and a bruise makes this movement painful. (c) Tight strapping restricts the rib cage's expansion and contraction, so air would move in and out of the lungs less easily. (d) Not tight strapping: it protects the ribs but restricts breathing; light support with rest is better, though the case for protection is real.

questions.q:
A trainer plans a week for a 50 kg student whose right knee is sore. Day 1: arm circles. Day 2: bending and straightening the knee while seated. Day 3: slowly turning the head from side to side. Day 4: standing still while tapping the head.
(a) Name the joint type used on each of Days 1 to 3.
(b) Which days involve the sore knee, and why?
(c) What range of weight is the student's skeleton, using 12 to 15 per cent?
(d) The trainer must drop one day to protect the knee. Which, and what is lost?
questions.a: (a) Day 1 ball and socket (shoulder); Day 2 hinge (knee); Day 3 pivot (skull and backbone). (b) Day 2, because the knee is the hinge joint being bent. (c) 6 kg to 7.5 kg. (d) Drop Day 2: it exercises the sore knee; the loss is the hinge-joint and leg-muscle practice. Dropping another day would not protect the knee.
